pages.text: No one mines these four. Germanium, indium and cadmium ride in sphalerite at tens to a few thousand grams a tonne, and gallium in bauxite at about fifty; each is taken out of a stream a zinc plant or an alumina refinery already runs. Here, as there, they are scarce.
pages.title: Byproduct metals

pages.text: Germanium. Two zinc leach residue, 500 mB of hydrochloric acid and 100 mB of chlorine, heated, give 100 mB of germanium tetrachloride, which boils out of the acid at 83 °C; the chlorine keeps the arsenic as arsenate, which stays behind.
pages.title: Germanium

pages.text: 250 mB of tetrachloride and 500 mB of water give a germanium oxide and 250 mB of the acid back, and two oxide with 500 mB of hydrogen in a heated vat reduce to two germanium ingots, at about 650 °C, below the metal's 938.

The first transistors were germanium. The alloy-junction transistor (General Electric and RCA, 1951) is an n-type germanium die with a dot of indium alloyed into each face: a plastic sheet deployed with a germanium nugget, two indium nuggets and a copper wire gives four of the Factory's transistors.
Most germanium now goes to fibre optics and infrared lenses, which the pack does not have.
Indium. Two zinc leach residue and 500 mB of sulfuric acid, heated, are the hot acid leach, 500 mB of indium sulfate liquor.
pages.title: Indium

pages.text: D2EHPA, our P204, takes indium out of a sulfate liquor before anything in it but ferric iron: 1,000 mB of liquor, 250 mB of P204 and 100 mB of hydrochloric acid in a vat with a mixer give 100 mB of indium chloride strip, and the 900 mB of raffinate go back to the zinc leach as zinc leach liquor; the organic comes back but for 5 mB.
100 mB of strip and two zinc nuggets cement an indium sponge, and two sponge electrorefined between two electrodes in a vat give two indium ingots.

Most indium goes into indium tin oxide, In2O3 with a tenth of SnO2, transparent and conducting, the electrode film on every flat screen: an indium ingot, a tin nugget and 250 mB of air, superheated, sinter to two, and in place of the Factory's silicon a segmented display built on it makes eight.

Gallium. Bauxite's gallium dissolves with the alumina and builds up in the liquor that goes round the refinery, to about 0.2 g/L. Pechiney took it out of the spent liquor on a mercury cathode, as gallium amalgam, and decomposed that in caustic to sodium gallate; refineries now use ion-exchange resins.
pages.title: Gallium

pages.text: 1,000 mB of spent Bayer liquor and a mercury in a vat between two electrodes give 50 mB of sodium gallate liquor and 950 mB of caustic soda for the digester, and the mercury comes back nineteen times in twenty.
250 mB of gallate liquor on two electrodes give two gallium nuggets and 200 mB of caustic. Gallium melts at 29.8 °C, in a warm hand.

The blue LED is indium gallium nitride on sapphire (Nakamura, Akasaki and Amano, Nobel Prize 2014), grown from gallium and ammonia near 1,000 °C: two gallium nuggets, an indium nugget, an alumina for the sapphire and 250 mB of ammonia in a heated vat give two LED chips.

A blue chip under a yellow phosphor, yttrium aluminium garnet with cerium, shines white: a chip, a yttrium oxide, a cerium oxide, a framed glass and two copper nuggets make six light bulbs. Gallium arsenide, the other half of gallium's use, wants arsenic, which the pack does not have.

Cadmium. The zinc dust that cleans the leach liquor brings the cadmium down as a sponge, and the cadmium sponge is a toxic dust: the itai-itai disease of the Jinzu valley was cadmium from a zinc mine. A sponge pressed in a heated basin melts to a cadmium ingot, at 321 °C.
pages.title: Cadmium

pages.text: Most cadmium went into nickel-cadmium batteries, which the pack does not have; the rest into cadmium yellow, the sulfide: an ingot and two sulfur dust, heated, give six yellow dye. Cadmium red wants selenium, which it does not have either.

Sources: USGS, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025, Germanium, Indium, Gallium and Cadmium; Ullmann's Encyclopedia of Industrial Chemistry, "Germanium and Germanium Compounds", "Indium and Indium Compounds", "Gallium and Gallium Compounds" and "Cadmium and Cadmium Compounds"; Sinclair, The Extractive Metallurgy of Zinc (AusIMM, 2005); Alfantazi and Moskalyk, "Processing of indium: a review", Minerals Engineering 16 (2003).
